To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two-dimensional treatment planning program has a number of limitations, and that some of these limitations may be remedied by the use of a computer graphics display.

the limitations of two-dimensional treatment-planning programs include a lack of involvement of the physician in defining the clinical situation, deficiencies in the algorithms used to calculate dose, failure to compute dose distributions throughout the volume of clinical interest, failure to provide tools to specify and verify the accuracy of treatment deliveries, and failure to provide estimates and displays of errors.

1) the algorithms used in two-dimensional treatment planning computer programs are deficient; 2) the programs are inadequate in their handling of noncoplanar beam arrangements; and 3) they fail to provide tools for estimating error, comparing rival plans, and verifying the accuracy and precision of dose delivery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving the capabilities of computer programs used for treatment planning in radiation therapy.

the development of computer programs for the planning of external beam radiation therapy which will provide the clinician with tools for the analysis of the problem, the formulation of a plan, and the verification that the plan is being carried out.
the development of tools to improve the quality of radiation therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
conventional two-dimensional computer planning programs are useful, but are not adequate for planning radiation therapy in the 1980's.
two-dimensional treatment planning systems, as they now exist, are not sufficiently accurate or complete to be used for planning radiation therapy.
conventional computer programs are inadequate for the task of planning radiation therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

conventional two-dimensional treatment planning systems are useful for planning treatments, but that they have limitations which should be considered when using these systems to design and verify treatments.
the two-dimensional planning programs currently available are inadequate for many of the problems that arise in radiation oncology.

the limitations of current computerized planning systems can be reduced by a more complete specification of the clinical problem, more sophisticated algorithms for computing dose, and more complete and accurate displays of the computed dose distributions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to improve the tools available for treatment plan evaluation, particularly in the area of error estimation.
the current generation of treatment planning programs are not adequate for the task of planning radiation therapy.
the use of two-dimensional treatment-planning systems should be limited to situations where there is no other choice, such as in the planning of treatment with electron beams.
